title: Helping Students Grow With AI
author: Steve Karandy
summary: Steve Karandy, working with high school seniors interested in AI, asks what a student can understand, explain or do more confidently on their own after using it. He draws on Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, which frames education as a patient process and calls for supporting teachers so students use technology responsibly, critically and creatively. His proposed approach starts with student thinking before any tool is opened, then uses AI to challenge a draft argument. Four questions guide the process: what do I think, what should I question, what can I verify, and what can I explain myself. He describes an AP US History lesson where students evaluated Gemini output and found both strong answers and errors, calling it AI Literacy 101. He adds privacy, access and approved-tool guidance and suggests Gemini Notebook as a teacher-controlled starting point, concluding that the aim is better thinkers rather than better prompt writers.
points: Students should write what they already think before opening an AI tool, so they have something of their own to examine.
Four questions (what do I think, what should I question, what can I verify, what can I explain myself) keep AI use tied to student reasoning.
Asking students to describe how they used a tool, what they changed and what they rejected gives teachers better material for feedback than a polished paragraph.
An AP US History lesson in which students checked Gemini output for errors illustrates practical AI literacy.
Privacy, access without paid subscriptions, and approved tools should shape classroom AI activities, with non-AI alternatives where they better serve the objective.
quotes: There is a practical question underneath that work: after using AI, what can a student understand, explain, or do more confidently on their own?

Before opening a tool, students could write what they already think, identify a question they cannot yet answer, and choose a skill they want to strengthen. That initial effort gives them something of their own to examine.
What do I think? Begin with an attempt, even when it is incomplete.
This was an excellent example of AI Literacy 101 and how we teach students that AI is a powerful tool, but we still need to understand that it is just that.

Students should be able to describe how they used a tool, what they changed, and what they chose to reject. That explanation gives teachers a better starting point for feedback than a polished paragraph alone.
A learning activity should allow meaningful participation without requiring students to buy a subscription or disclose information they would rather keep private.
We do not want students to use AI for the sake of AI or be better prompt writers, we want them to be better thinkers and innovators.
